beats.text: The first mathematical invention was not a formula.
beats.section: About 30,000 years ago — a scratch on a bone

beats.text: It was just a scratch, carved into a bone.
beats.section: About 30,000 years ago — a scratch on a bone

beats.text: In the Czech Republic, archaeologists found a wolf bone with notches cut into it, about thirty thousand years old.
beats.section: About 30,000 years ago — a scratch on a bone

beats.text: And in nineteen fifty, in central Africa, they found a baboon bone covered in notches arranged in groups, about twenty thousand years old.
beats.section: About 30,000 years ago — a scratch on a bone

beats.text: It is called the Ishango bone.
beats.section: About 30,000 years ago — a scratch on a bone

beats.text: It sounds simple, doesn't it? But this may be the biggest leap of all.
beats.section: About 30,000 years ago — a scratch on a bone

beats.text: Because for the first time, people pulled the quantity apart from the things being counted.
beats.section: About 30,000 years ago — a scratch on a bone

beats.text: Before, three sheep were simply three sheep.
beats.section: About 30,000 years ago — a scratch on a bone

beats.text: After the notches, three sheep, three days, and three moons could all be written the same way: three marks.
beats.section: About 30,000 years ago — a scratch on a bone

beats.text: That is the jump from counting things to the idea of number itself.
beats.section: About 30,000 years ago — a scratch on a bone

beats.text: And in a sense, all of mathematics since then is that same move, made again and again: pulling the idea away from the stuff.
beats.section: About 30,000 years ago — a scratch on a bone

beats.text: But notches have a problem.
beats.section: About 3000 BC — Sumer

beats.text: If you need to record four hundred and thirty-seven sheep, you can't carve four hundred and thirty-seven lines.
beats.section: About 3000 BC — Sumer

beats.text: About five thousand years ago, the Sumerians of Mesopotamia invented the first written numerals.
beats.section: About 3000 BC — Sumer

beats.text: One sign for one, another for ten, and another for sixty.
beats.section: About 3000 BC — Sumer

beats.text: They counted in base sixty, not base ten.
beats.section: About 3000 BC — Sumer

beats.text: Why sixty?
beats.section: About 3000 BC — Sumer

beats.text: Because sixty divides evenly by two, three, four, five, six, ten, twelve, fifteen, twenty, and thirty.
beats.section: About 3000 BC — Sumer

beats.text: That makes it wonderful for sharing out land, grain, and time.
beats.section: About 3000 BC — Sumer

beats.text: And here is the fun part: Sumer is still alive in your daily life.
beats.section: About 3000 BC — Sumer

beats.text: An hour has sixty minutes, a minute has sixty seconds, and a full circle has three hundred and sixty degrees, which is six times sixty.
beats.section: About 3000 BC — Sumer

beats.text: So every time you check a clock, you are using an invention that is five thousand years old.
